content: An audiologist should be actively involved in every aspect of a hearing-screening program, particularly at the statewide implementation level and, whenever feasible, at the individual hospital level. Hospitals and agencies should also appoint a physician to oversee the medical components of the Early Hearing Detection and Intervention (EHDI) program. Each team responsible for hospital-based Universal Newborn Hearing Screening (UNHS) programs should evaluate the hospital's infrastructure in relation to the screening program. Hospital-based programs must consider several factors, including the type of screening technology (e.g., Otoacoustic Emissions [OAE] or automated Auditory Brainstem Response [ABR] testing), the validity of the specific screening device, the timing of the screening relative to nursery discharge, the availability of qualified screening personnel, the suitability of the acoustic and electrical environments, follow-up referral criteria, referral pathways for follow-up, information management, and quality control and improvement. Reporting and communication protocols must be clearly defined and should include the content of reports to physicians and parents, documentation of results in medical charts, and methods for reporting to state registries and national datasets. Physiologic measures must be used to screen newborns and infants for hearing loss. These measures include OAE and automated ABR testing. Both OAE and automated ABR technologies provide noninvasive recordings of physiologic activity underlying normal auditory function, are easily performed in neonates and infants, and have been successfully used for UNHS. However, there are significant differences between the two measures. OAE measurements are obtained from the ear canal using a sensitive microphone within a probe assembly that records cochlear responses to acoustic stimuli. Thus, OAEs reflect the status of the peripheral auditory system, including the cochlear outer hair cells. In contrast, ABR measurements are obtained using surface electrodes that record neural activity generated in the cochlea, auditory nerve, and brainstem in response to acoustic stimuli delivered via an earphone. Automated ABR measurements reflect the status of the peripheral auditory system, the eighth nerve, and the brainstem auditory pathway. Both OAE and ABR screening technologies can detect sensory (cochlear) hearing loss. However, both technologies may be affected by dysfunction in the outer or middle ear. As a result, transient conditions of the outer and middle ear may lead to a failed screening result despite normal cochlear and/or neural function. Additionally, because OAEs are generated within the cochlea, OAE technology cannot detect neural dysfunction (e.g., eighth nerve or auditory brainstem pathway disorders). Therefore, neural conduction disorders or auditory neuropathy/dyssynchrony without accompanying sensory dysfunction will not be detected by OAE testing. Some infants who pass newborn hearing screening may later develop permanent hearing loss. This loss may reflect delayed-onset hearing loss, and both ABR and OAE screening technologies may miss certain types of hearing loss (e.g., mild or isolated frequency region losses). Criteria for interpreting pass/fail outcomes should be based on clear scientific rationale and evidence. Screening technologies that incorporate automated-response detection are essential to eliminate the need for individual test interpretation, reduce the effects of screener bias or operator error on test outcomes, and ensure consistency across infants, test conditions, and screening personnel. When statistical probability is used to make pass/fail decisions, as is the case for OAE and automated ABR devices, the likelihood of obtaining a pass outcome by chance increases with repeated screenings. This principle must be integrated into rescreening policies. There are no national standards for the calibration of OAE or ABR instrumentation. This issue is further complicated by the lack of uniform performance standards. Manufacturers of hearing-screening devices do not always provide sufficient evidence to validate the specific pass/fail criteria or automated algorithms used in their instruments. In the absence of national standards, audiologists must obtain normative data for the instruments and protocols they use. The Joint Committee on Infant Hearing (JCIH) recognizes that there are important differences between screening performed in well-infant nurseries and that performed in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU). Although the goals in each setting are the same, numerous methodological and technological issues must be considered in program design and pass/fail criteria. In well-infant nurseries, many inpatient screening protocols provide for one hearing screening and, if necessary, a repeat screening before hospital discharge using the same technology both times. Either technology used in the well-infant nursery can detect peripheral (conductive and sensory) hearing loss of 40 dB or greater. When automated ABR is used as the sole screening technology, neural auditory disorders can also be detected. Some programs use a combination of screening technologies (e.g., OAE testing for the initial screening followed by automated ABR for rescreening) to reduce the fail rate at discharge and the subsequent need for outpatient follow-up. With this approach, infants who fail an OAE screening but pass an automated ABR test are considered a screening pass. Infants in the well-infant nursery who fail automated ABR testing should not be rescreened using OAE testing and passed, as these infants are presumed to be at risk for a subsequent diagnosis of auditory neuropathy/dyssynchrony. In the NICU, which is defined as a facility where a neonatologist provides primary care for the infant, newborn units are categorized into three levels: Level I (basic care, well-infant nurseries), Level II (specialty care for infants at moderate risk of serious complications), and Level III (units providing both specialty and subspecialty care, including life support such as mechanical ventilation). Surveys have identified 120 Level II NICUs and 760 Level III NICUs in the United States, and infants who have spent time in the NICU represent 10% to 15% of the newborn population. The 2007 JCIH position statement includes neonates at risk for neural hearing loss (e.g., auditory neuropathy/dyssynchrony) in the target population to be identified in the NICU, as evidence suggests that neural hearing loss results in adverse communication outcomes. Consequently, the JCIH recommends ABR technology as the only appropriate screening technique for use in the NICU. Infants who do not pass automated ABR testing in the NICU should be referred directly to an audiologist for rescreening and, when indicated, comprehensive evaluation, including diagnostic ABR testing, rather than for general outpatient rescreening. Screening results should be communicated to families immediately so they understand the outcome and the importance of follow-up when indicated.
